Results update as you type. Bar size, spacing and laps come from your engineer's drawings.

  • ASTM A615 nominal bar weights
  • Shows how stock bars and laps are counted
  • Runs in your browser

How to use the rebar calculator

  1. Enter the slab length and width, the bar spacing and the edge cover (the distance from the slab edge to the outer bars).
  2. Choose the bar size and the stock length you can buy.
  3. Check the lap length. The default of 40 bar diameters is a common rule of thumb, not a code value: the lap on your engineer's drawings always governs.

Formula

  • Bars along the length: round up ((width − 2 × cover) ÷ spacing) + 1, each (length − 2 × cover) long. Bars along the width are counted the same way. Rounding up keeps the real spacing at or below the spacing you enter.
  • When a bar is no longer than a stock bar, as many pieces as fit are cut from each stock bar. When it is longer, stock bars are joined with lap splices: stock bars per line = round up ((bar length − stock length) ÷ (stock length − lap)) + 1, and each lap adds its length to the total.
  • Weight = total length × weight per footmeter. ASTM A615 nominal weights: #3 0.376, #4 0.668, #5 1.043, #6 1.502 lb/ft.Metric bars: kg/m = d² ÷ 162 (steel at 7850 kg/m³): 10 mm 0.617, 12 mm 0.889, 16 mm 1.580 kg/m.

Example: a 10 × 10 ft slab, #4 bars at 12 in, 3 in cover, 20 ft stock bars: (120 − 6) ÷ 12 = 9.5, rounded up to 10, + 1 = 11 bars each way, each 9.5 ft long. 22 bars × 9.5 ft = 209 ft, × 0.668 lb/ft = 139.6 lb (63.3 kg). Two 9.5 ft pieces fit in each 20 ft bar, so buy 11 stock bars.

Example: a 6 × 4 m slab, 12 mm bars at 300 mm, 75 mm cover, 12 m stock bars: 14 bars of 5.85 m and 21 bars of 3.85 m, 162.75 m in total, × 0.889 kg/m = 144.7 kg. Two 5.85 m pieces or three 3.85 m pieces fit in a 12 m bar, so buy 7 + 7 = 14 stock bars.

Bar sizes

US bar numbers are eighths of an inch: #4 = 1/2 in (12.7 mm). The ASTM soft-metric name of #4 is #13, of #5 #16; they are not the same as 12 mm or 16 mm metric bars.

What is not counted

  • This is one layer of bars in a grid. Dowels, hooks, chairs, ties and cutting waste are not included.
  • Bar size, spacing, cover and lap length must come from your drawings or a structural engineer.

Sources

  • ASTM A615 nominal bar weights and diameters, as listed in South Dakota DOT Construction Manual, Chapter 7, Table 7.1.
  • Metric kg/m from steel density 7850 kg/m³ (π ÷ 4 × 7850 ÷ 10⁶ = 1 ÷ 162.2).

FAQ

How do I calculate how much rebar I need?

Count the bars each way with (side − 2 × cover) ÷ spacing, rounded up, + 1, multiply by the bar length, then add laps. A 10 × 10 ft slab with #4 at 12 in needs 22 bars, 209 ft, 139.6 lb.A 6 × 4 m slab with 12 mm bars at 300 mm needs 35 bars, 162.75 m, 144.7 kg.

How much does rebar weigh?

ASTM A615 nominal weights are #3 0.376, #4 0.668, #5 1.043 and #6 1.502 lb per foot.Metric bars weigh about d² ÷ 162 kg per meter: 10 mm 0.617, 12 mm 0.889, 16 mm 1.580 kg/m.

How long should a rebar lap be?

It depends on the bar, the concrete and the design; your drawings or a structural engineer set it. 40 bar diameters is only a common rule of thumb, and it is the default you can change here.

Why is the edge cover subtracted?

Bars must stay inside the concrete for corrosion and fire protection, so the grid starts one cover distance in from each edge.

Is #4 rebar the same as 12 mm?

No. #4 is 1/2 in (12.7 mm), named #13 in ASTM soft metric. It is slightly heavier than a 12 mm bar.
